John Spilsbury
jon SPILZ-ber-ee
proper noun
Spilsbury, an English place-name surname (Oxfordshire); John, Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

Biblical Definition

John Spilsbury (c. 1593–c. 1668) was, by the best account, the pastor of the first Particular Baptist congregation in England, gathered in London about the year 1638 out of the separatist churches, when a company of believers, persuaded from Scripture that baptism belongs to disciples and not to infants, resolved to obey their Lord in the ordinance He appointed. A cobbler by trade and a labourer in the Word, Spilsbury led this flock to recover believers’ baptism at a time when to do so was to court reproach, ejection, and peril. He set his convictions in print, defending in his treatise on the ordinance that the subjects of baptism are professing believers and its true mode a burial with Christ, answering with Scripture those who pressed the baptism of infants. These first Particular Baptists were Calvinistic to the bone, and from their number and their confessions would flow, in the next generation, the great Second London Confession of 1689 which the churches own to this day. Spilsbury stands therefore as a forefather of the whole Reformed Baptist people: a man who counted obedience to Christ’s plain command dearer than the peace of conformity, and who, gathering a church upon the rule of the Word, planted a seed from which a mighty tree of confessing, baptizing, gospel-preaching congregations has grown.

Webster 1828 Definition

Pastor (c. 1593–c. 1668) of the first Particular Baptist congregation, gathered in London about 1638.

expand to see more

The reputed pastor of England’s first Particular (Calvinistic) Baptist church.

Gathered his London congregation about 1638 out of the separatist churches.

A cobbler by trade who recovered believers’ baptism from Scripture.

Author of a treatise defending baptism as the ordinance of professing disciples.

A forefather of the Reformed Baptist people and the 1689 Confession that followed.

Key Scripture

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Act 2:41 — "Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls."

Rom 6:4 — "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life."

Act 8:37 — "And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his labour recovers the ordinance of believers’ baptism.

expand to see more

Spilsbury is preserved because he stood, at cost, upon the plain command of Christ: that baptism follows faith and pictures a burial with the risen Lord. Where the churches of his day pressed the baptism of unconscious infants, he gathered a people to obey the Great Commission as it is written, teaching the nations and baptizing the taught.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is believers’ baptism—that the ordinance belongs to those who gladly receive the word, and signifies death to sin and newness of life in Christ. Spilsbury’s courage summons the churches to prize obedience to Scripture above the comfort of custom, and to guard the ordinances Christ Himself appointed as the badges of a professing, regenerate church.

Hebrew Roots

Spilsbury’s ministry roots the Baptist confession in the scriptural recovery of believers’ baptism.

expand to see more

The Great Commission’s order—teach the nations, then baptize (Mat 28:19).

The baptism of those who “gladly received his word” (Act 2:41).

Baptism as burial with Christ into newness of life (Rom 6:4).

The requirement of heart-belief before the ordinance (Act 8:37).

The 1638 London church as seedbed of the 1689 Confession.

Usage

"“Spilsbury gathered the first Particular Baptist church about 1638.”"

"“He defended believers’ baptism in print against the paedobaptists.”"

"“From his little flock flowed the whole Reformed Baptist tradition.”"
